bio.en: Tristan de Montebello is co-creator of Ultraspeaking, the best public-speaking workshop Lenny has found, and a former world-championship finalist in public speaking.
bio.zh: Tristan de Montebello 是 Ultraspeaking 的联合创造者——这是 Lenny 所见过最好的公开演讲工作坊——他也是世界演讲锦标赛的前决赛选手。

summary.en: Tristan shares how to become a dramatically better, more comfortable speaker, including speaking on the spot without panic. He explains the mindset and reps that build speaking confidence, why most fear is learned, and how communication accelerates your career. The episode is a practical, energizing guide to a skill that pays compounding dividends.
summary.zh: Tristan 分享了如何成为显著更优秀、更从容的演讲者，包括在毫无准备下临场发言而不慌乱。他解释了构建演讲信心的思维与练习、为何大多数恐惧是习得的，以及沟通如何加速你的职业生涯。本期是一份务实、令人振奋的指南，关乎一项带来复利回报的技能。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: I actually think that the biggest misconception with tackling your speaking is that people grossly underestimate just how transformative it could be to your life. And the reason it's so transformative is because speaking is not a specialized skill, it's a meta skill. That means that the better you get at speaking, the better your life gets. (00:06:16): So an example of a meta skill is fitness, for example. If you were to start saying, "Okay, I'm going to transform my fitness," and you start lifting weights and you start going on runs, obviously your muscles are going to get bigger, you're going to get more in shape, and your cardiovascular system is going to improve. But that's actually only a sliver of the impact it's going to have on your life because you're going to start feeling more energy, and you're going to start having these nice hormones, these endorphins flowing through your body and you're going to feel better about yourself. And when you walk in front of the mirror, suddenly you're going to have a boost in confidence. So naturally, everything else in your life is going to start to improve as a result of you focusing on your fitness. And for speaking, it's the same thing. (00:07:01): This blew my mind when I went on my own speaking journey, is when I started making breakthroughs in speaking, other things started to feel different. So as you get breakthroughs, how you feel at work feels different. How you feel in your group of friends feels different. How you feel in a group of strangers, especially, how you feel and your family can even be impacted. This seeps into everything else in your life. But the thing is, because there's so much self-consciousness that goes with speaking, we often feel kind of constraints under the layers of overthinking and anxiety that come with speaking. So it can be hard to realize that underneath these layers, you actually have this extraordinary superpower, because as humans we're evolved to speak, this is what we are. So you don't need to teach a baby how to speak, it will learn by itself with no formal education. So what that means is, we all have this incredible hardware. (00:08:12): The thing is, over the course of our life, because of all these little situations that happen, we start getting bugs in the software and we're not really upgrading our software. The moment you get the bugs and things start working, not working, we start avoiding, and suddenly it's like we're not upgrading our software anymore. So we're stuck on old, buggy software. But the reality is, let's not forget that we have incredible software that were evolved for this. So all we need to do is some debugging and some upgrading of the software and suddenly your entire life can change. So that's really one I want to impart on anybody listening. You have it in, you already have what it takes.
turns.zh: 实际上，我认为在提升口语表达能力方面，人们最大的误区在于严重低估了它对生活产生的变革性影响。之所以说它具有变革性，是因为口语表达并非一项专业技能，而是元技能。这意味着你越善于表达，生活质量就越高。 （00:06:16）：以健身为例，就是一项元技能。如果你开始对自己说：“好，我要改变自己的身体素质。”然后开始举重、跑步，显然你的肌肉会变得更强壮，身体素质会提升，心血管系统也会得到改善。但这只是它对生活影响的冰山一角，因为你会开始感到精力充沛，体内会涌动着让人愉悦的激素——内啡肽，你会自我感觉良好。当你站在镜子前时，自信心会瞬间飙升。因此，当你专注于健身时，生活中的其他方面也会随之改善。口语表达也是如此。 （00:07:01）：在我踏上口语表达之路时，最让我震惊的是，当我在口语表达方面取得突破时，其他方面也随之发生了变化。比如，在工作中，你的状态会变得不同；在朋友圈里，你的表现会更出色；在陌生人群体中，尤其是面对家人时，你的状态也会受到影响。这种改变渗透到生活的方方面面。但问题在于，由于口语表达伴随着太多的自我意识，我们常被过度思考和焦虑的层层包裹所束缚。因此，很难意识到在这些表象之下，你其实拥有非凡的超能力，毕竟人类天生就具备说话的能力。 （00:08:12）：但在生活中，由于各种小状况的堆积，我们的软件开始出现故障，却又不愿升级。当故障出现，功能失常时，我们开始回避，仿佛再也无法升级软件。然而现实是，我们拥有为此进化而来的惊人硬件。我们只需进行一些调试和升级，生活就能焕然一新。这就是我想传递给每位听众的真谛。你本就具备所需的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So kind of building on what you just talked about, some of this insight of, your life can improve and how you kind of always have to unlearn stuff. One of my favorite maybe core insights and tenets of the way you approach teaching people to speak, is you talk about how if you don't enjoy speaking, you're doing it wrong. And that really helped me because you kind of encourage, you kind of remind people, try to have fun as you're doing. Can you just talk about that insight and why that's important and how that helps people become better?
turns.zh: 好的。基于你刚刚提到的观点，你提到生活可以得到改善，以及人们总是需要摒弃旧有观念。关于你教人们口语表达的方法，我最喜欢的核心见解之一，就是你说如果不享受口语表达，那就是做错了。这对我帮助很大，因为你鼓励人们，提醒他们要享受这个过程。你能谈谈这个见解的重要性，以及它如何帮助人们变得更出色吗？

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Well, I think that's very tied to what you were saying. I see enjoyment as a barometer, if I'm doing things right, I'm probably enjoying myself. If I'm doing things wrong, particularly with speaking, because again, this is something we're naturally evolved to do. So if we're naturally evolved to do it, it's not something that we dislike doing. It has to be something that rewards us. So as soon as things start not feeling enjoyable, it's a sign, hey, I'm probably doing this wrong, guy. There's something here that I'm doing that is making this unenjoyable that's probably not helping me. (00:10:03): And I think you mentioned that in those people who can hold an audience who are really good communicators in business, it looks like they feel very comfortable, it looks like they feel like themselves. And if you think about speaking, when you're talking with your kids, or with your partner, or with your best friend, your childhood friend, your parents, ever, we all have environments where we feel completely like ourselves. And when we do, communication is extraordinarily enjoyable. It's just a means to connect with other people, a means to share what we have on our mind and it's very, very empowering and it feels very good. (00:10:42): Then I take the same person with the same skill set and the same ability and I bring them in a business setting, and suddenly I don't feel like myself anymore. And because of the pressure, I start trying to speak differently. So people start having, I'm going to try to think really hard of what I need to say and I want to control the words that are going to come out of my mouth before they come out of my mouth so I make sure I don't make a mistake. And you basically loop in this thing that is so counter what communication is, which is just a natural subconscious scale. So using speaking as a barometer of, hey, if this is not feeling good, I'm probably overthinking. I probably need to relax and try to just feel a little bit more like myself. (00:11:27): But this also applies to practice, where in your practice, because this is not an overnight thing, you can't just snap your fingers, read a book, and be a better speaker. Well, your practice has to be enjoyable as well because otherwise two weeks in, you're going to quit just like a shitty fitness journey or diet. Right? You have to find joy in it and it has to be structured in a way where it rewards you as well, so that you get more energy and you get more enjoyment while you do it.
turns.zh:
嗯，我觉得这和您之前所说的密切相关。我把享受乐趣视为一个晴雨表。如果我做得对，通常就能享受到乐趣；如果做得不对，特别是演讲方面——毕竟这是我们天生擅长做的事。所以如果我们天生擅长某件事，那就说明我们并不讨厌做这件事。它必须能给我们带来回报。所以一旦事情开始让人失去乐趣，这就是个信号，嘿，我可能做错了。这里肯定有某个环节让我失去了乐趣，而这对我的帮助并不大。

（00:10:03）：我记得您提到，在那些能够掌控听众、在商业场合沟通能力出色的人身上，他们看起来非常自在，仿佛做回了自己。再想想演讲，当你和孩子、伴侣、好友、童年伙伴、父母交谈时，我们总能在这样的环境中完全做回自己。而当我们这样做时，沟通变得无比愉快。它只是一种与他人建立联系的手段，一种分享心声的途径，既能赋予我们力量，又令人倍感满足。

（00:10:42）：然后我让同一个人拥有同样的技能和能力，却把他们带入商业环境中，突然间他们就不再是自己了。因为压力的缘故，他们开始试图用不同的方式说话。比如，他们会开始绞尽脑汁思考接下来要说什么，想要在话语出口前把控好每个字，确保不犯错。而这恰恰与沟通的本质背道而驰——沟通本该是一种自然而然的潜意识级别的行为。把演讲当作衡量标准——如果感觉不好，说明我可能想得太多了。我或许需要放松下来，努力找回真实的自己。

（00:11:27）：但这同样适用于练习环节。毕竟这不是一夜之间就能掌握的，你不能指望一拍脑袋、读本书就能成为更出色的演讲者。你的练习也必须充满乐趣，否则两周后你就会像放弃糟糕的健身计划或节食一样放弃。是的，你必须从中找到乐趣，并且练习方式也要能给你带来回报，这样你才能在过程中获得更多能量和乐趣。

But right before we get there, are there any other core insights or principles or lessons that are fundamental to the way you found that it works to become a better public speaker, that kind of inform a lot of the stuff we're going to be talking about?

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: The day I understood that speaking was a subconscious flow-oriented process and not a conscious process, completely changed the way I approached it. So instead of thinking tactics and frameworks and adding more to the outside of the things I need to think about, when I realized when I speak best, I'm actually not thinking about speaking. It's the last thing I think about is the speaking part. I'm completely in tune with whatever it is I'm trying to convey to my audience or the person in front of me. And the goal is to get into a flow state and stay in that flow state all the way through the finish line. That's what really, really changed my mindset about speaking, because then it changes all of the exercise, the exercises you want to do. It changes how you can think about speaking. (00:13:24): And one of the ways that changed how I practiced was, instead of focusing on the symptoms of speaking, I started to try and figure out, well, what are the root causes that create these symptoms, and can I address those? So instead of counting my filler words, if that's something that's annoying to me, I'm going to go back and try to figure out, well, what's the root cause of that? Well, the root cause of having lots of filler words or racing in your speaking, is that you probably struggle to feel comfortable slowing down, relaxing, or even pausing when your mind is racing and you feel pressure. Solve that, and not only do the filler words take care of themselves, but the racing takes care of itself and you suddenly have more mind space. (00:14:11): And if you feel super constrained in your speaking, very monotonous, then maybe you feel boxed in and you're struggling to allow yourself to feel to be all of what you are under pressure because there's probably a lack of certainty. A lack of trust in, hey, if I let myself be more intense or if I let some of these emotions pop out, or if I take a time to gather my thoughts, is everything going to unravel, or is that going to work for me? And if you haven't proven that to yourself, then you're just going to go for safety and so you're going to be very monotonous and constrained, and that's creates monotony. But if I can solve that, suddenly I have freedom. So thinking through this and understanding that the goal here is upgrading the software and it's really layering, taking all the bad habits away and putting in new habits that I can just stay in this flow state without getting pulled out, that really changes the game.

直到那一天，我才意识到说话其实是一个潜意识驱动的流畅过程，而非有意识的努力。这彻底改变了我的说话方式。于是，我不再费心思去思考策略和框架，也不再刻意添加多余的修饰。当我发现自己说话最顺畅的时候，我甚至没有刻意去思考如何说话——相反，我最先考虑的是如何准确传达信息，如何与听众或对面的人建立心灵共鸣。关键在于进入流畅状态，并在整个过程中保持这种状态。这真正改变了我的说话思维模式，因为它彻底重构了整个训练体系，重塑了人们对说话技巧的认知。

（00:13:24）其中一个关键转变是，我不再关注说话的表象，而是开始追根溯源，思考问题的根源并寻求解决方案。比如，如果我对口语中的填充词感到厌烦，我会反思：这些填充词的根源是什么？其实，过多使用填充词或说话语速过快的原因，是因为当大脑高速运转、压力重重时，我们难以放慢节奏、放松身心或适当停顿。只要解决了这些问题，不仅填充词会自然消失，语速也会随之放缓，思维空间也会随之扩大。

（00:14:11）如果说话时感觉非常拘谨、单调，可能是因为我们被困在思维框架中，无法在压力下展现真实的自我。这源于缺乏安全感——我们怀疑：如果放开自己、释放情绪、静心思考，事情会不会失控？如果没有亲自验证过这些假设，我们就会选择安全路线，结果只能机械地重复旧模式。

但只要破解了这些思维障碍，自由感就会随之而来。通过拆解旧习惯、植入新习惯，我们就能持续保持流畅状态。这才是真正的突破。

实际上我之所以会想到这个点，是因为一旦你意识到演讲更多关乎根本原因——比如玩那些能从根本上改变你的游戏，而不是关注表象——你就会发现自己分享的纯粹战术建议和框架少了很多，因为我们试图从大脑进入潜意识。（00:16:10）所以当我思考这个问题时，我想到了三点想分享的。第一点能让你看起来更出色，第二点能让你听起来更出色，第三点能让你感觉更自在。  

第一点是让你看起来更出色。这听起来很基础，但很多人都有这个坏习惯。当我试图整理思路或思考时，人们往往会低头看手机。如果你在Zoom上这样做，效果会更糟，因为看起来你在看手机或笔记，但即使是面对面交流，这样做也会显得缺乏自信。这样一来，你会不自觉地传递出一种信号：哦，这个人在这里有点不确定，或许他会停下不说话，反而更容易被打断。（00:16:56）  

如果你改变这个习惯，开始向上看。我建议向右上方看，但你可以朝任何方向看，只要抬头看，就能自然而然地显得深思熟虑。比如朝天花板看。这意味着你看起来更自信，因为任何愿意在演讲中停顿的人都是自信的人。因此，你被打断的可能性大大降低。这只是一个小调整，但效果显著。  

唯一的问题是，如果你不习惯这样做，如果这不是你的习惯，那么第一次这样做时会感觉有点不自然，可能也不会刻意去注意。所以我建议把“思考上”写在便利贴上，贴在电脑上，方便提醒自己。这样做几次后，这就会成为新的习惯，自然而然地让你看起来更自信。

Before they finish, they start getting pulled out of flow. And this is the same feeling of you're running at school and you see the finish line and just a few yards before you start slowing down. It's just, I don't know, we're built that way. (00:18:53): And in speaking, it's the same thing. People tend to give a great answer and then either they kind of taper off at the end, which doesn't leave you with a good impression, or they'll actively say the doubts that are coming up in their mind of maybe they'll be giving a great answer and then suddenly they say, "I don't really know if that makes sense."

看起来更自信。现在如何听起来更自信。这是一个非常重要的问题，这个概念叫做“强势收尾”。我们之所以要提到这个，是因为大多数人往往收尾不力。为什么会这样呢？科学家曾让即兴说唱歌手接受功能性磁共振成像（fMRI）扫描，结果发现，他们必须进入深度流畅状态。当即兴说唱时，你有节拍，但没有歌词，必须即兴创作歌词、旋律等。这时你别无选择，只能全神贯注。研究发现，他们大脑中某个特定区域会亮起，这表明他们进入了流畅状态。而当接近尾声时，大脑会突然兴奋起来，甚至在结束前就开始退出这种状态。这就像你在学校赛跑时，看到终点线却在最后几米时放慢脚步的感觉。说白了，我们天生就这样。

（00:18:53）在演讲中也是如此。人们往往会给出很棒的回答，但要么在结尾时逐渐收尾，让人留下不好的印象，要么会主动表达出内心的疑虑，比如突然说：“我不确定这是否说得通。”

turns.en: Yeah, but what the thing is, what happens when you do that? When you do that, it's like you're forcing this lens on your audience, where now even if they had the best of experiences with your answer, now they're looking at everything you said through the lens of, oh, this person was kind of uncertain. So it's like you had a very smooth flight across the Atlantic and your landing was absolutely horrible. You were bumpy when you were coming up, and then when you hit the landing, you bounced three times and you thought you were going to die. You're not going to remember the smooth flight, you're going to remember the ending. So a simple tactic here is, anticipate that as you get to the end of anything you're saying, you're going to naturally start regaining consciousness and you're going to start being a little bit more self-aware, and some of those uncertainties are going to pop up. Know that it's coming and make sure you land the plane. (00:20:14): So what that looks like is, either you just make your ending sound like an ending and then leave it at that, or you can prompt your brain. You can use summary prompts, this is incredibly powerful. It just means you say the beginning of a sentence or the beginning of, yeah, the beginning of a sentence, and your brain's going to fill in the gap. It's going to. You're prompting your brain and your brain will always deliver. So you get to the end, you're like, okay, I got to wrap up now. And so you'll say, "So to wrap up..." And your brain's going to fill in the gap. Or, "In summary, so my point here is, so what I want you to remember," and you just place those words and your brain's naturally going to do the work of closing it for you. But make sure you don't let go of the gas pedal at the very last moment, you need to land that plane.

是啊，但关键是，这样做会有什么后果？当你这样做时，就好像在给听众强加一个框架。即使你的回答原本很出色，现在人们也会通过这个框架来评判你，觉得你最后有些不确定。就好像你飞越大西洋时一路顺畅，但着陆时却糟糕透顶。起初平稳，后来颠簸不已，最后更是弹跳三次差点丧命。人们记住的不是平稳的飞行，而是糟糕的结局。所以一个简单的方法是，当你即将结束任何演讲时，要预料到自己会自然地开始恢复清醒，注意到一些不确定的念头。这是必然的，要确保自己能完美收尾。

（00:20:14）具体做法是，要么让你的结尾听起来就是结尾，然后结束，要么可以提示大脑。使用总结提示词非常有效。就是在句子开头或段落开头稍作停顿，大脑会自动填补空白。比如你说：“所以总结一下，”或者“简而言之，我的观点是，”然后把这些词说出来，大脑会自然地帮你完成收尾。但关键是最后一刻别松开油门，要确保完美着陆。

turns.en: Yeah. The third one is staying in character. And these go hand in hand. And what's really powerful is when you start doing these, there's a beautiful feedback loop that happens that gives you a lot of confidence. So staying in character I said is the one that's going to make you feel more confident. (00:21:33): What's staying in character? So it's related to end strong in some sense, in that people tend to self-sabotage a lot. I'm speaking, and obviously as I'm speaking, all of my senses are really, really heightened. So I'm aware of everything, if a word comes out a little bit weird or if it's not the word that I was expecting to hear come out of my mouth, I'm going to be very aware of that because I was expecting something and something different happens. But that happens all the time when speaking. I'm starting to not make as much sense or I feel like I'm rambling, going a little bit too long. All of these create insane noise in the back of my mind, the insecurities. And you have a choice there, because I can tell you right now, nobody can tell. People cannot see what you feel, even though it feels that way when you feel really, really strongly, but people can't see it. You're just looking like a normal speaker, competent and confident. But internally, it feels like everybody can see. (00:22:34): So you're feeling all this insecurity and it feels like there's an elephant in the room. And so what most people do is they start leaking and they break character. And they'll say, "Oh, man, I'm not making sense right now," or they'll laugh nervously after saying a word that came out weird, which is kind of saying like, "Oh, I also noticed that this word came out weird and it's okay." Right? Or they'll keep letting all of the insecurities and doubts come out when people didn't see it in the first place. So again, it's like I'm forcing these filters onto my audience and now they can only see me through that light. (00:23:15): And so one analogy I love for this is, again, a flying analogy. You're on the plane, everything's smooth, you're having a great time watching your movie, and suddenly you're interrupted by the pilot who picks up the intercom and says, "Oh, ladies and gentlemen, so I just had a red light start blinking here in the cockpit, and I'm not sure what this is. It could be really bad, honestly, but I don't know. So don't worry, please, I'll get back to you soon." First thing that's going to happen if you experience that is you're going to think, I wasn't worrying in the first place. But then you start thinking, wait, something probably is going wrong. And now the smallest noise, the tiny little bit of turbulence, a creak on the right, you're going to start thinking, oh no, we're going to die, every time. (00:24:03): So you're going to make any little mistake, any little imperfection, you're going to turn that into something big. That's what happens when you speak. If you start leaking and letting the insecurities come out, people are going to start thinking, this person doesn't really know what they're talking about. It's like a leader who isn't clear in their direction. Suddenly I'm thinking, wait, I think I have to second guess everything here because I'm not sure about this guy or this person. (00:24:33): And the good news is, the solution is very, very simple. The solution is that is just, don't share your insecurities. Put your best foot forward and stay in it the whole time. Stay in character from beginning all the way through past the ending, because you go all the way through your speech, then you got to end strong, which is a form of staying in character, and then let it be. And that's so important, just let it be and you're going to notice something incredible. If you're the type of person who would break character a lot, start staying in character, and the cue use for myself is, stay in it. And the worse it gets, the more I'll say, just stay in it. And what happens is, you stay in it. (00:25:21): And you expect everybody at the end to say, "Oh my God, you looked so uncomfortable, what was happening?" But people can't see that, that you look confident. So they're just going to give you the reaction that a confident person would get, and you're going to notice, oh wow, I am coming off as confident, and that's going to make you feel more confident. And so it's a very reinforcing cycle. If you start staying in character and ending strong, naturally, you're going to be reinforced by this behavior and you're going to realize, oh, I didn't need to break character. I didn't need to hedge every time I spoke, and that's going to give you much more confident, and you're going to start realizing, people just look confident by default. This is a crazy thing. I want everybody to walk around the world and look at people and think, most of the people I'm looking at are actually nervous right now. You're going to look at them and you're like, I can't tell. Most people speaking up in meetings are feeling a level of nervousness, but you can't tell unless it's through the roof.

是的。第三点是保持角色状态。这两者是相辅相成的。真正强大的地方在于，当你开始做到这些时，会形成一个良性循环，让你获得极大的自信。所以我说的保持角色状态，正是能让你更有自信的关键。（00:21:33）：什么是保持角色状态？这和"完美收尾"在某种程度上是相关的，因为人们往往会自我破坏。我在演讲时，显然所有感官都高度敏锐。所以我能察觉到任何异常，比如某个词说得有点怪，或者脱离了预期表达，这时我会格外留意。但演讲时这种情况时常发生——比如开始语无伦次，或者感觉自己啰嗦不已。这些都会在脑海中引发焦虑的声音，让你怀疑自己。而你其实可以选择不理会这些，因为没人能看得出来。人们看不到你的内心波澜，即便你自己感觉强烈，但别人只能看到一个正常、自信的演讲者。（00:22:34）：所以你感受到所有不安，感觉有个大象在房间里。但大多数人会开始露出破绽，打破角色状态。他们会说："天，我现在说话都乱七八糟了"，或者在说出奇怪词汇后紧张地笑，这其实是在说："哦，我也注意到这个词说得怪，但没关系"。对吧？或者他们会继续暴露不安和疑虑，而这些其实本就无人察觉。所以我就像是在给听众强加滤镜，让他们只能透过这个滤镜看我。（00:23:15）：我喜欢的比喻是飞行模拟。你在飞机上，所有都顺顺利利，正看电影时，突然被飞行员打断，他拿起对讲机说："女士们先生们，驾驶舱里红灯闪烁，我不确定是什么问题，但可能是很严重的情况。不过别担心，很快回来汇报。"如果你经历这种情况，最初的反应可能是：我本来就没担心。但随后你会开始思考，等等，可能真出问题了。现在最微小的声音，最细微的颠簸，右边传来的吱吱声，你都会开始想，天哪，我们要死了。每次都这样。（00:24:03）：所以你会放大任何小错误，任何不完美，让它们变成大问题。演讲时就是如此。如果你开始露出不安，让这些情绪显现，人们会开始怀疑你是否真的懂行。这就像一个方向不明确的领导者。突然我会想，等等，我得重新评估每件事，因为我不确定这个人能否胜任。（00:24:33）：好消息是，解决方法非常简单。就是别暴露自己的不安。全力以赴，始终保持角色状态。从开头到结尾都要保持角色状态，因为你要贯穿整个演讲，然后用力收尾。
这是一种保持角色状态的方式，然后顺其自然。这非常重要——只要顺其自然，你就会发现令人惊喜的变化。如果你是个经常出戏的人，那就开始保持角色状态吧。我给自己定的口号是：“保持角色状态。”情况越糟糕，我就越会说：“继续保持。”结果发现，你真的能做到。（00:25:21）最后，你可能以为大家会说：“天啊，你看起来好不自在，到底发生了什么？”但人们看不到你的不安，他们只会把你当作自信的人来反应。你会惊讶地发现：“哇，我看起来真的很自信！”这会让你更加自信。这是一个良性循环。如果你开始保持角色状态并完美收尾，自然会得到正向反馈。你会意识到：“我根本不需要打破角色状态。每次发言时也不必犹豫不决。”这会让你更加自信。你会开始发现，大多数人天生就看起来很自信。这太不可思议了。我希望每个人在世界上行走时，都能观察周围的人，并意识到：我看到的大多数人此刻其实都很紧张。你看着他们，可能觉得“看不出来”。大多数在会议上发言的人其实都感到紧张，但除非紧张情绪极度外露，否则根本看不出来。

And I think the reason I do this and the reason I think a lot of people leak, which I love that term of just I don't leak, that you know, feel something's not going right. The reason I do it is I feel like me being upfront, I know this isn't great-
turns.zh: 我喜欢这样做，但我也深知自己在这方面有过错。我觉得自己之所以会这样做，之所以会让很多人暴露出自己的不足，原因在于当我坦诚面对现实时——我知道这并不理想——

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... makes it okay, but in reality, that's hurting you because it's like when I watch standup comedy. When the comedian's like, "Oh, sorry, that bombed," if he didn't say that or she didn't say that, I'd just forget about it, and we'd move on to the next thing. And it brings all this attention to, oh, I see, okay, it's not going great. Otherwise, you're just like, all right, whatever, I didn't like that joke. And so, yeah, I guess any thoughts on just that, why people do this?
turns.zh: ……这看似无伤大雅，但实际上却在伤害你自己。就拿看单口喜剧表演来说，当喜剧演员说"哦，抱歉，这段太烂了"时，如果他不说出来，或者她不说出来，我们可能很快就忘了，继续看下一个片段。但当你把注意力引向"哦，原来大家都看出来了"时，整个局面就变了。原本大家只会想"好吧，不管了，反正我不喜欢这个笑话"。但现在你却把注意力引向"大家都发现了这个问题"，于是人们的注意力瞬间转移。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Well, I think that's exactly that. It's because you're convinced that everybody can tell. And so two things will happen. Either they could tell because it was a big thing and everybody could tell, but you shining light on it is literally that. It's like, hey, everybody, you're driving a train, everybody's in the train, you're the driver as the speaker, everybody's going with you. So if there's a crash on the side of the road, you can keep going and they'll not be looking at the crash a second later and they'll be looking at the next landscape, or you can stop the train and tell everybody, "Hey, let's look at this crash here real quick. I'm so sorry about it." When you keep going, people will forget it in a second and they're not going to pay attention to you. And with the peak end rule, what we we're seeing, people remember the end of experiences more than they remember the beginning of experiences. So you're going to be left with that feeling at the end. (00:27:58): The other piece is, because most people won't notice it in the first place, they'll be in their own minds. So when you share this, you're popping their bubble. And so I see people speaking all the time where I'm super in tune with the feeling I'm getting when they're speaking. I'm listening to the energy, I'm listening to everything that's happening, so I can try to understand, what state are they in right now? So when I get woken up from that state of somebody saying, "Oh man, can I go again right now? That really sucked." It's even more visible for me. (00:28:36): And I'll often have to say, "Hey, man, I was so into what you were saying," and I'll poll the audience, "is anyone surprised?" And everybody every time is like, "No, I thought that you were doing great. I was completely with you." So that's the case most of the time, but because we're convinced that people can tell, we want to break that fourth wall or because something happened and we know people can tell, we want to acknowledge it so it doesn't feel like I'm the only one in the room who can't tell that something went wrong here. But this habit of saying, "No, I'm going to be confident, I'm leading, I'm going to keep us going in a certain direction," is extremely powerful and very self-reinforcing.
turns.zh: 这就是关键所在。是因为你坚信别人能看出来。而接下来会发生两件事。要么是因为事情本身太明显，大家都能察觉，但你把它公之于众，这无异于告诉所有人"嘿，火车出轨了，大家都在车上，司机是你，演讲者。而你继续前行时，人们很快就会忘掉这件事，不会关注你。而根据"高峰终结法则"，我们发现人们更容易记住经历的结尾，而非开端。所以最终你只会留下那种糟糕的感觉。（00:27:58）另外，因为大多数人原本并不会注意到这些，他们都沉浸在自己的世界里。所以当你分享这些时，就是在打破他们的幻想。我经常观察人们演讲时，能准确捕捉到他们的情绪变化。我倾听他们的能量，留意每个细节，这样就能理解他们当下的状态。当有人突然说"天哪，我现在能再来一次吗？太糟糕了"时，这种情绪就更明显了。（00:28:36）我常不得不说"嘿，兄弟，我刚刚完全沉浸在你的演讲中"，然后问观众"有人感到惊讶吗？"每次大家都会说"不啊，我觉得你表现得很棒，我完全跟得上你的思路"。大多数情况下都是如此。但因为我们坚信别人能看出来，所以想打破第四面墙，或者因为某件事已经发生，我们想承认它，这样就不会觉得自己是唯一一个察觉到问题的人。但这种"不，我要保持自信，我要引领方向"的习惯，极其强大且能自我强化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so let's actually show people what this looks like by actually doing some live games. I know one of your principles for Ultraspeaking is you can't learn to speak by not speaking. You need to practice speaking to get better at speaking, and these games are a way to actually do that in a really fun way. So maybe first of all, just why games? When I did this course, I was just like, huh, because it's a bunch of games. I thought this was a public speaking course. So maybe talk about just why you approach it through games, everything you do is a game in this course.
turns.zh: 好的，那我们就实际演示一下这些活动是什么样子吧。通过玩一些实时游戏，我相信你们都听说过Ultraspeaking的一个核心理念——不说话就无法学会说话。要想提高口语能力，就必须不断练习说。而这些游戏就是以一种非常有趣的方式来实现这一目标的。那么首先，选择游戏的原因是什么？我当初参加这个课程时，心里还纳闷，啊？因为课程里全是游戏啊。我原本以为这是一门公开演讲课程。所以不妨先讲讲为什么要通过游戏来学习。毕竟在这门课程里，每个环节都是以游戏的形式呈现的。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Yeah. Well, the first piece of the puzzle is what you were saying, that you can't get better at speaking without speaking. And it's, intuitively you could think, everybody knows that if you want to become a great cook, you can't just read 100-
turns.zh: 是的。首先，关键点在于你提到的，不说话就无法提高口语能力。这听起来很直观，但仔细想想大家都知道，要想成为一名出色的厨师，光看书是不行的。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Everybody knows that if you want to become a great cook, you can't just read a hundred cookbooks. You actually have to spend most of your time in the kitchen refining your intuition, testing things, experimenting, learning new recipes, and building your timing and everything that goes with it. But in speaking, we tend to do the opposite, probably because it's a little bit scary and because there aren't that many options out there to practice the speaking itself. There aren't that many environments where you can do it right now. So we're kind of left with nothing, so, "Okay, I'll just go read an article or watch a YouTube short and hope that's going to make a difference." (00:30:38): But maybe the bad news is, you have to do it. You have to ask yourself, "Am I going to be serious about taking on speaking and making a difference here?" And if you are, then you're going to have to do the thing. You have to practice speaking. But the good news is, it's only the outside that's scary. As soon as you get started, you're going to get rewarded. And then, the better you get at it, the more enjoyable it becomes. (00:31:03): So why games then? Well, games number one, are fun to play. And as I was saying earlier, if your practice is not fun, you're going to stop. So you need intrinsic reward with what you're doing. But what all of the Ultraspeaking games have in common is that it's short, deliberate practice, short reps followed by feedback, followed by another rep. So that was more important than the idea that it was a game at first. (00:31:35): When we started coaching with Michael Gendler, my co-founder, it was just him and me in my backyard with somebody in front of us testing things out. And we would say, we would give him a speech title just to get a baseline. "Okay, what's the most incredible invention in the world?" And we'd watch this person go into their mind and start freaking out. And they'd think, " The iPhone," and then, "I don't know the iPhone. That's pretty recent. So maybe it's fire. Is it fire though? Was there a bigger maybe communication? I don't know. Wait. Maybe we've evolved for communication." (00:32:08): And the longer they spent thinking, the worse their answer tended to be, and the more their confidence tended to go down as they were speaking. So then we said, "Well, we've got to get this person speaking right away." So we'd say, "I'm going to ask you another question, but just start speaking." And so, I'd ask them another question and they couldn't start speaking right away. (00:32:27): So we just tried to compress it more and more and more to turn it into something where then it was like, "I'm just going to say a word and you have to say something about it, so horses." "Horseback riding is fun because you can go places." "Cats." "Cats are crazy because if they were bigger, they would eat you." And I just, almost like word association. Let's get words out. (00:32:46): Then we started developing different games for everything. Every root cause we were seeing, every symptom we were seeing, we'd figure out the root cause and we'd create some sort of a way to get the person into it as quickly as possible. And it's just one day, six months in that we realized, "Hey, did we just create a game? This feels like a board game." And then we created, I have this, we created Speak Before You Think, the game for people who think too much, and this is a bunch of cards with all of our games. And then, Covid hit and we turned it into online games.
turns.zh: 众所周知，若想成为一名出色的厨师，光是阅读几百本烹饪书籍是远远不够的。你必须在厨房里花费大量时间，不断磨练直觉、进行试验、学习新菜谱，掌握时间把握能力以及相关技能。但在口语表达方面，我们往往反其道而行之，或许是因为这项任务令人望而生畏，且缺乏有效的练习机会。目前几乎没有现成的环境能让我们即刻投入实践。因此，我们往往束手无策，只能说：“好吧，那我就去读篇文章或者看看YouTube短视频，指望能有所帮助。”（00:30:38）但或许坏消息是，你必须亲自行动起来。你得问自己：“我是否真的要认真对待口语表达，并在这个领域有所建树？”如果你的答案是肯定的，那就必须付诸实践。口语练习的乐趣至关重要。正如我之前所说，若练习过程毫无乐趣，你注定会半途而废。因此，你需要从练习本身获得内在奖励。所有超口语游戏的共同点在于：短暂而高效的练习——快速重复、即时反馈、再重复。这种循环机制比游戏属性本身更为重要。（00:31:35）当我与联合创始人Michael Gendler开始执教时，我们只是在后院面对面进行模拟演练。我们会给学员一个演讲主题以获取基准：“世界上最伟大的发明是什么？” 对方往往陷入沉思，举手投降：“iPhone吧，但我对iPhone不熟悉。太新了。或许是火。火算吗？还是通信方式更重要？我不知道，等等，或许我们是为了交流而进化的。” （00:32:08）思考时间越长，答案质量越差，口语表达信心也随之下滑。于是我们决定让学员即刻开口：“再问你个问题，现在就开始说。”结果对方还是无法立刻开口。（00:32:27）我们不断压缩练习时间，最终演变为：只需说出一个词，比如“马”，对方就必须即兴发挥：“骑马很有趣，因为能去很多地方。”“猫太疯狂了，如果它们体型更大，会吃掉你的。” 这几乎成了词汇联想游戏。（00:32:46）后来，我们针对每个问题开发了不同游戏。针对每个症结和症状，我们都会找到突破口，让学者尽快进入状态。短短六个月，我们突然意识到：“我们是不是刚发明了一款游戏？这感觉像桌游。” 于是诞生了专为深度思考者设计的游戏《先说再想》，以及包含所有游戏的卡牌集。随后新冠疫情来袭，我们将游戏转为线上模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, I didn't know that.
turns.zh: 哦，我不知道这个。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Yeah. The magic of games is short reps, immediate feedback, practice feedback, practice feedback. And it's enjoyable, you get rewarded, you get to adjust as you go. And what's changing is your internal feeling as you're going. So you're learning lessons, but you're internalizing. All of the practice is happening through speaking.
turns.zh: 是啊。游戏的魔力在于短暂的重复、即时的反馈、练习反馈、练习反馈。它很有趣，你能得到奖励，还能随时调整策略。关键在于你内心的变化——你在学习的过程中不断内化知识。所有的练习都是通过口语完成的。

turns.en: To reinforce what you just shared, I haven't shared this with you, but after I took the course, the mini course, I went to see my family in L.A. We visited for a few days, and I was talking about this course and just how fun it was and interesting and how much I learned from it. And it was just, we spent like an hour just doing this and everyone loved it.
turns.zh: 为了强化你刚才分享的内容，我还没跟你说过，但我上完那门课程后，参加了一个迷你课程。之后我去洛杉矶看望家人，我们一起待了几天。我跟他们聊起这门课，讲它有多有趣、多有意思，以及我从中学到了多少东西。我把游戏调出来，因为我能在线访问相关内容。我就问：“嘿，你们想试试吗？”然后我们开始玩一些即将介绍的游戏。结果我们玩了整整一个小时，每个人都乐在其中。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everyone just felt so much better about their public speaking. Afterwards, my mom was like, "Hey, how do I do that on my own later?"
turns.zh: 每个人对公开演讲的信心都增强了。之后，我妈妈问：“嘿，我之后怎么自己也能这么做呢？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's cool.
turns.zh: 哇，太酷了。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: My sister's like, "I want to start doing open mic nights because that was really fun just to talk."
turns.zh: 我妹妹说：“我想开始参加开放麦之夜，因为那真的很有趣，只要开口说话就行了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nice.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: So were you actually coaching them? How were you walking them through the different games?
turns.zh: 那你实际上是在指导他们吗？你是怎么一步步带他们玩不同游戏的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We just pulled them up and played them. And then, I shared some of the tips that I learned in the class that we took, just like, "Try it this way" or "Try not to focus on being correct. Just focus on confidence and not leaking that you're not doing great." All these things we're going to talk about. Yeah. So it was a lot of fun. So let's get into some of these games. So we're going to try two or three. Which one do you want to start with?
turns.zh: 我们就把游戏调出来玩。然后，我分享了我们上课学到的一些技巧，比如“试试这种方法”或者“别太在意正确性，专注于建立自信，别暴露出自己做得不好的地方”。这些内容我们都会讲到。真的很有趣。现在让我们开始玩几个游戏吧。你想先从哪个开始？

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Conductor maybe.
turns.zh: 指挥家吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. I love Conductor. That one was really insightful to me.
turns.zh: 太好了。我喜欢指挥家这个游戏。它对我很有启发。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Okay, so I've got Conductor. The way this game works is that when I click "start training," I'm going to have a random title that's going to appear. And for those of you who are just listening and not watching this, Lenny will say the title out loud so you can hear. And then, what you won't see or what you'll see if you're watching is in front of me, all I'm going to see are a series of random numbers. It's going to start with five, and five is just my natural rate of speaking like I'm speaking right now. But then, I might see a number from one to 10, and each one of these numbers represents an intensity or a state that I have to tap into. So if I see a seven, I automatically have to raise my voice and get into that kind of an energy. And if I see a 10, you could only imagine what that is. But it's also true for the lower ones. If suddenly I see a three, I have to find a way to calm my energy and match the three and go all the way down to one. (00:36:00): And then, there might be a slide that says "breathe," which is just an indication to pause. And when I see that slide "breathe," if I just go silent, that's because I'm in front of the breathe slide and I'm not allowed to speak. And in that moment, my goal is just to relax myself and calm myself and then see what happens where I'm at when that slide moves on to the next one. And now we're going to do this. This is going to be 70 seconds, so it's going to be super quick. Ready?
turns.zh: 好的，我现在用的是Conductor这款工具。游戏的玩法是这样的，当我点击“开始训练”时，会随机出现一个标题。对于正在听但没看屏幕的听众，Lenny会把标题大声读出来，方便你们听到。而对于正在观看的观众，你们会看到在我面前的一系列随机数字。数字会从5开始，这是我正常的说话语速。然后可能出现1到10的数字，每个数字代表一种情绪或能量状态。比如看到7，就要提高音量进入那种状态；看到10，你们可以想象那意味着什么。但低数字的要求同样严格，比如3，就要想办法平复情绪，匹配数字3，直至降到1。（00:36:00）接下来可能会出现“呼吸”的提示牌，表示暂停。当我看到这个提示牌时，如果我保持沉默，那说明我正处于呼吸提示牌的区域，不能说话。此时我的目标是放松自己，调整状态，等提示牌转到下一页时再观察进展。现在我们开始练习。时间限制70秒，速度很快。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So I'll read the title as soon as it pops up.
turns.zh: 好的，我一看到标题就读出来。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: "When I grow up."
turns.zh: “当我长大后。”

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: When I grow up, I want to have taken on all of my weaknesses or all of the emotional things that are holding me back. Because kind of annoying for me that I'm 40 years old and there's still things that are holding me back that man, I've had these when I was a kid. I was like this when I was 10. And it drives me crazy, because aren't I supposed to be an adult? Aren't I supposed to be mature and have my life together? I have two kids. I have this incredible responsibility. And I have to teach them, I have to show them the way. So I've decided I'm going to hire a coach, and I talked to him just a couple of days ago, so this is perfect timing because I want to unwrap, unravel, and untwine every single one of these emotional blockers so that when I grow up, I'm completely free.
turns.zh: 等我长大后，我想克服所有弱点，或者说摆脱那些阻碍我的情绪问题。让我很烦恼的是，我已经40岁了，却还有这些阻碍我的情绪问题。这些问题我在10岁时就已经存在了。这真让我抓狂，因为我不是应该是个成年人了吗？不应该成熟稳重，生活井井有条吗？我有两个孩子，肩负着重大的责任，还要教导他们、为他们指引方向。所以我决定聘请一位教练，几天前刚和他聊过，这真是天时地利，因为我想剖析、解开、化解每一个情绪障碍，这样等我长大后，就能彻底自由了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was so fun to watch. I'm seeing the numbers. If you're on YouTube, you can see what's going on there. If you're not, basically there's different numbers that give Tristan the different energies to be at, and that was masterful.
turns.zh: 看这个太有趣了。我能看到数字。如果你们在YouTube上观看，能看到Tristan的各种情绪变化。他太厉害了。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: I think we saw, what did we see? We saw a six. It went up first, six, seven, then it went down to three. Then we saw, I think a two, a one, then a breathe, and then it went back to a five. How about you give it a go and then we chat.
turns.zh: 我记得我们看到过哪些数字？先是6，然后升到7，接着降到3。接着是2和1，最后是“呼吸”提示牌，再降到5。你们不妨自己试试看，然后我们再聊。

turns.en: Let's do it. What do you think?
turns.zh: 开始吧。你们觉得怎么样？

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Ladies and gentlemen, let's see this. Here we go. The title is The Greatest Puzzle.
turns.zh: 女士们先生们，让我们见证奇迹。开始吧。标题是《最伟大的谜题》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The greatest puzzle that I think that I've had in my life, and I think just for most people, is trying to figure out what to do with their life. And I just had to spend so much time thinking... Actually, no, let me change. I'm changing direction. I actually have known from very early on what I wanted to do with my life. I've actually found it to be not much of a puzzle. I knew from pretty early that I wanted to be a software engineer. And interestingly, I became a software. （00:53:19）

(01:25:22): And you start just creating this alien stack of paper with all of your ideas of what your talk might be, and then you're left with 10, 15 pieces of paper. And now as the deadline comes closer, what do you have to do? And they're still in writing mode. They're not in your mind. (01:25:50): So now that I've created that script that I spent a lot of time editing, now I have to memorize it. And memorization is pretty. We're not good at memorization. Robots are good at memorization, humans are not. And memorization is like a chain where you just have all of these links very linearly. And everybody knows the feeling of going through, reciting a poem as a kid, and suddenly you miss one verse and you're lost, and now you're a deer in the headlights. (01:26:21): So what we're doing with the Accordion Method is instead of preparing our talk by writing, we're going to prepare our talk by speaking, and we're going to do so in a very specific way where we're going down the accordion to create extreme clarity, and to understand what the essence of our talk is, and then back up the accordion to bring back in intentionally just the right pieces. (01:26:48): So I was thinking of an analogy for this, and one that I really like is imagine you're redecorating your living room. So I might be left with that one couch that I really love, a pillow, a beautiful light that I bought three years ago, and one or two other small things. And as I look at that, I'm going to have clarity on the vision I want for my living room. And then very slowly, very intentionally, I'm going to go take certain elements that were already there that I might want to bring back in, and I'm going to bring new elements that now I see make sense. 好吧，说这话可能有点偏颇，但我觉得"手风琴法"或许是我这辈子最引以为傲的成果之一，因为它几乎彻底颠覆了我们对演讲准备的传统观念。（01:24:19）：到目前为止，我们主要讨论的是即兴演讲，而即兴演讲将占据你绝大多数的演讲场景。大概80%的演讲内容都是无法提前准备的。但有时候你会面临截止日期，必须要发言——无论是工作面试、向CEO汇报，还是向全团队或千人听众做演讲。（01:24:45）：我认为传统方法简直糟糕透顶。它太不靠谱了，而且我还没发现有其他创新方案能超越它。这让我和迈克尔抓狂不已，最终催生了"手风琴法"。传统方法是什么？就是演讲临近了，我把所有想法堆在几张纸上。然后试着调整结构，在调整过程中灵感不断涌现。比如，"或许我该这么说"，或者"我不想遗忘开头提到的那个点"。（01:25:22）：最后，你会积累一堆杂乱无章的纸条，等到截止日期临近，又得忍受把十几张纸变成脚本的折磨，生怕遗忘那些精心润色的金句。可脚本毕竟是文字，不是活在你脑海中的东西。（01:25:50）：费尽心思编辑好的脚本还要背诵，而人类向来不擅长背诵。背诵就像一连串线性排列的环节，任何环节出错都可能让你手足无措。（01:26:21）：手风琴法的核心是用演讲代替写作来准备演讲。具体流程是：沿着手风琴展开的路径，先极度清晰地理清演讲核心，再有条不紊地收纳关键要素。（01:26:48）：我曾为此打个比方：想象你在重新装修客厅。传统方法是写十页纸然后背诵，就像你看着客厅随意调整家具，把可能用得上的东西堆在角落，再费力拼凑新元素。手风琴法则说：想象家具也能这么简单，把所有冗余都清除，只留下最核心的元素。比如你心爱的那张沙发、三年前买的漂亮台灯，以及一两件小物件。审视这些核心后，你的思路会豁然开朗。

（01:28:15）：那么这如何与手风琴法相结合呢？我们会先进行第一步。如果你愿意，可以把所有这些想法写在纸上，以便把它们从脑海中释放出来。这完全没问题。但从现在开始，就不再有剧本了。我只举个例子，说明时间限制的具体操作。我们通过时间限制来展开手风琴式演练。例如，你可以说：“我要讲三分钟。”然后设置一个计时器，并遵循两个规则：一是全程保持角色状态，二是以强有力的结尾收尾。所以你必须坚持到三分钟结束，无论讲得多糟糕，犯多少错误都没关系。关键在于把我的想法用口语表达出来。这样我就能充分调动大脑，明确自己的真实想法。

（01:29:38）：最后再降到一分钟，最后降到30秒。从三分钟的演讲开始，一路精简到30秒。当你讲到30秒时，你只会留下客厅里的沙发和台灯这些核心元素。当这些核心元素确定后，你就能清晰地把握演讲的主旨，而且随着过程的推进，主旨可能还会发生变化。

理解你的演讲内容可能在你沿着“手风琴曲线”推进过程中有所变化。从当前位置开始，我们将再进行30秒的练习，然后继续沿着“手风琴曲线”向上推进。接下来，你再进行30秒的练习，然后延长至1分钟、2分钟，一直到3分钟。每一步都从30秒逐渐过渡到1分钟。最初，1分钟的时间感觉很困难。现在，这已经是之前的两倍了。因此，你可以引入与你想分享的演讲内容相契合的元素，然后延长至2分钟，同样步骤。到达3分钟时，曾有客户表示感觉脑海中像有整个足球场那么广阔的空间。现在，无论剩下多少演讲内容，都能清晰、专注地传达出来。

（01:30:45）不仅如此，这正是这种方法令人惊叹之处——你的演讲内容已经内化于心。此前，你可能需要按照传统方式编写并反复润色演讲稿，最终还要背诵。但现在，你只需专注于演讲核心，整个过程会自然而然地完成。（01:31:22）现在，你可以用1分钟、2分钟、3分钟、5分钟的时长进行演讲。这种方法极具灵活性。无论你犯错，都无伤大雅，因为你对演讲内容了如指掌。这不是机械背诵，而是真正理解后的自然呈现。

通过这种方法，你不仅清晰构建了演讲框架，还在演讲前期就进行了深度打磨。到最后，你能准确传达核心信息，做好舞台演示的准备。

I guess where do you fit this in the workflow so that you actually remember what you want to say when it comes time?
turns.zh:
关于“手风琴曲线”中的三分钟练习环节，我亲身经历过那种感觉——“哇，时间怎么这么充裕”。关键在于，你会把精力集中在最重要的核心要点上，然后有时间对这些要点进行深化，同时剔除无关紧要的部分，比如冗长的开场白。现在你只需直切主题，再逐步展开。这对我非常有效，是一次深刻的启发。

（01:32:19）对于想实际应用这个方法的人来说，比如即将进行演讲、一周后要做全员汇报的人，是否要提前一周开始？还是提前几天？如何将这个方法融入工作流程中，确保到演讲时能准确传达信息？

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: I can't say do it exactly a week or two weeks or it really depends how well familiar you are with the content. If you have an all hands, and this is something that you've been hashing with your executive team over the past two months, you probably know it really, really well and you have a lot of clarity and now it's just about organizing it nicely. So in that case, maybe you want to do a rough go through the accordion a week ahead of time so you have a clear sense of, "What is it that I want my audience to remember and what are the pillars that I know I like to hit that feel really good?" (01:33:15): So you can think about these as the foundational pillars that support that one thing that you're sharing or bookmarks that I know I have to hit and then what I would like to do. And so that's what I would write down. I wouldn't write a script. I'd write those down. And then before the all hands, maybe the day before, maybe even the morning of, depending on how important this is or how comfortable you feel, then you might go through just one or two reps of it, but now you already know it, so it should come back very, very quickly in your mind.
turns.zh: 我没法确切地说一周或两周后，但这真的取决于你对内容的熟悉程度。如果你要做全员会议，而这个内容过去两个月你一直在和高管团队讨论，那你可能对它非常熟悉，思路清晰，现在只需要把它组织得更流畅。所以在这种情况下，也许你想提前一周快速浏览一下提纲，这样就能清楚地知道："我希望听众记住什么内容？哪些关键点是我想重点强调、感觉很棒的？"（01:33:15）：你可以把这些视为支撑你要分享的核心内容的基本支柱，或者是必须提及的要点，接着再写下自己的想法。我不会写脚本，只会把这些要点记下来。然后在全员会议前一天，甚至当天早上（取决于事情的重要性或你的舒适度），你可以再通读一遍，但因为你已经熟悉内容，所以很快就能回想起来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it sounds like it's okay to have some bullet points at the end. It's hard for me to imagine going on stage with a bunch of people watching, not have any slide, bullet point, speaker notes. Any problems just having a couple of the bullet points of core points next to me?
turns.zh: 听起来在最后加上一些要点是没问题的。我很难想象站在台上面对一群观众，却没有任何幻灯片、要点或讲稿。只是在旁边放几条核心要点的要点会有问题吗？

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Before a talk, I might have four things written down. My one thing, and we'll talk about this in the bow and arrow, my one thing, the one thing I want people to remember and then the three bookmarks or pillars that I want to hit. And these are kind of cues or reminders that are going to send me into that part of the speech. So for example, if I'm talking about the accordion method, like what I just said, if I go back and I think through the pillars of this one. Well, my one thing would be the accordion method is more powerful than memorizing and then doing it the old way. (01:34:35): And then my bookmarks might be number one, describe the old way or the old way. Number two, the new way or the accordion method. And then number three might be internalize, don't memorize, and that'll be kind of the takeaway. (01:34:53): And if I have that in my mind, if I have 30 seconds, I can say the old way sucks because you have to work so hard and memorize everything and you're memorizing written stuff, the accordion method is much more powerful because you are going to compress it and go down and then open it up and then I'll explain that in a second and then I'll say, so you're internalized not memorized. What I realized right now is actually, it's funny enough though, those were the bookmarks there, so that sent me down that path. But actually I would say bookmark number two is probably the living room analogy. So it would be the old way sucks, the living room analogy, and then describe the accordion method.
turns.zh: 在演讲前，我可能会写下四个要点：我的核心观点（我们在"弓箭法"中会详细讨论）、我想让听众记住的一件事，以及我要强调的三个要点或支柱。这些要点就像提示或提醒，能让我顺利进入演讲的各个部分。例如，如果我要讲"手风琴法"，就像我刚才说的，如果我回顾这个方法的三个支柱。那么我的核心观点就是手风琴法比死记硬背和传统方法更有效。（01:34:35）：然后我的三个要点可能是：第一，描述传统方法或旧方法。第二，新方法或手风琴法。第三，内化而非死记硬背。这就是关键要点。如果我牢记这些，要是只有30秒时间，我可以说："旧方法很糟糕，因为你得费力死记硬背所有内容"，而手风琴法则强大得多，因为你可以先压缩内容，再展开讲解，接着我会解释，然后说："所以你要内化而非死记硬背。"我现在意识到，实际上挺有趣的是，这些要点就是之前列的书签，所以这让我找到了正确的思路。但实际上我觉得第二个要点可能是"客厅类比"。所以顺序应该是旧方法很糟糕，客厅类比，然后描述手风琴法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's cool. That was an awesome example of just the insights that appear by forcing yourself through this exercise. And it sounds like maybe the best use of this method is if you have a talk all of a sudden short term it's coming, all of a sudden you have to give a talk somewhere. There's a really powerful method to come up with a great talk that's maybe tomorrow, which you didn't expect.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这是一个绝佳的例子，说明通过强迫自己完成这个练习，灵感就会涌现。听起来这个方法最适合在紧急情况下使用，比如突然要在明天做演讲，却毫无准备。它能快速帮你构思出精彩的演讲内容。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: When I say I love this, I use this for myself, I use this with every single client I work with regardless of if it's a five-minute talk, a 20-minute keynote, we're using the accordion method, and you can use this at the macro level or at the micro level, so you can use it for the whole talk, but you can also say, "Hey, let's hone in on this part one that you're struggling with or part two and let's use the accordion to get clarity there." (01:36:26): So you can use the accordion as almost like a brainstorming way. I just want to see where I end up here and it takes maybe 15 minutes or something to go through a full accordion. It depends the time constraints you give yourself. Sometimes I'll just do two minute, one minute 30 seconds, that's even shorter, but I'll go through it for one piece of the puzzle or it's like, "Hey, we're almost there. Let's really internalize it. Let's clarify this. Let's get it really, really tight." And then I might say, "Okay, now let's do the whole thing through the accordion. So your 20-minute talk, I want to hear it in three minutes." That gets really, really interesting.
turns.zh:
当我说我喜欢这个方法时，我自己也会用它，无论是与客户沟通五分钟，还是进行20分钟的主题演讲，我们都会用到手风琴法。这种方法既可以应用于宏观层面，也能用于微观层面。你可以将其用于整个演讲过程，但也可以针对某个你正纠结的部分，比如第一部分或第二部分，利用手风琴法来理清思路。
（01:36:26）：所以你可以把手风琴法当作一种头脑风暴的方式。我只想看看最终效果如何，完整完成一次手风琴法可能需要15分钟左右，具体时长取决于你的时间限制。有时我只用两分钟或一分半钟，甚至更短，但我会针对某个难点部分进行练习，或者在接近尾声时说：“嘿，我们快完成了。让我们真正理解它，理清思路，做到精确无误。”然后我可能会说：“好的，现在让我们用手风琴法把整个演讲过一遍。所以你20分钟的演讲，我希望你在三分钟内讲完。”这会变得非常有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. Anything else along the accordion method before we talk about the final technique before we wrap up?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。在结束前，我们能否再讲讲手风琴法的最终技巧？

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: We have a full self-paced course on ultra speaking on the accordion. I think it costs like 30 bucks or something like that to access all of the games and all the platforms. A bunch of them are free, but I think this one's behind the paywall. But we also put together a resource where we go all the way, we describe all of the accordion method, the bow and arrow, staying character ending strong on a free email course that we put together. That's ultraspeaking.com/Lenny. So this is shameless self-promotion, but if you want it to go grab it there, you can grab it there and then the bow and arrow is going to tie into the accordion method as well.
turns.zh: 我们有一个关于超演讲手风琴法的完整自学课程。访问所有游戏和平台大概需要30美元左右。其中很多是免费的，但这个课程是付费的。不过我们也整理了一份资源，全面讲解了手风琴法、弓箭法以及如何在免费的电子邮件课程中保持角色魅力并强势收尾。我们把它放在ultraspeaking.com/Lenny这个页面。这算是毫不避讳的自我宣传，但如果你感兴趣，可以去那里获取资料。弓箭法也会与手风琴法相辅相成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I'm glad you mentioned all that and we'll point people to that URL in the show notes. Okay, final topic is the bow and arrow technique. Let's talk about what that is and how folks can use that to give better talks.
turns.zh: 太好了。很高兴你提到了这些内容，我们会在节目笔记中附上相关链接。好的，最后一个话题是弓箭法。我们来讲讲这是什么方法，以及人们如何运用它来提升演讲质量。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: The bow and arrow starts with a, it's really a mindset shift that most of us are in the weeds, so we're very sensitive and familiar to all of the content that we're working on. If you're in data, then you have all of the data. If you're sharing ideas, you still have all of the ideas. And the mistake that most people do when they're preparing a talk, a presentation, an all hands a meeting, whatever it is we tend to focus more on what we want to say than what we want our audience to remember. So the mindset shift here is stop focusing as much on what you want to say and focus more on what you want your audience to remember. (01:38:51): What we found out is if you think about your last all hands, the last big meeting, the last talk you saw on YouTube or in person, you probably don't remember much. In fact, I wager you might only remember one thing from that talk. And that's what this is all based on. We call it the bow and arrow technique because we think you can only remember one thing out of a talk and that it's very powerful to go through that framework or that kind of thinking when you're building a talk. And the one thing is your arrow. And so when you have that one thing to me I say it's literally a single sentence that is the only sentence people would remember if they left your talk. Would you be satisfied with that sentence? (01:39:37): It takes some times to get to a good one, but if you have a good one, it unlocks everything. It's like you're having a north star or a compass in your pocket. You can always pull it out. You always know where you're going. It gives you a lot of clarity. It's also giving a lot of clarity to your audience obviously. (01:39:54): But you can't just throw an arrow at somebody's face. You need to notch it in the bow and pull the bow back. And so to pull the bow back, you need to add in weight to that sentence. And that often comes in the form of an interesting anecdote or a data point that's going to support that or a story that's going to add emotion or illustrate it. So you want to find ways in which you can give weight or pull back the bow so that your arrow has that much more impact. So usually the process of clarifying what your arrow is is a back and forth between the bow and the arrows. So if you're going down the accordion method after the first one you might write or before the first one, you might write a tentative arrow, "Here's my one thing", and then the next one you say, "Okay, actually my one thing might be a refined version of that." (01:40:55): And so you might rewrite it a little bit and then you might tentatively put in what you think the bow is. "I like the anecdote I used here. I like this data point that I thought was powerful and maybe I can end on this story or this call to action." Then you'll put that in and then you go back in and you give that a try and that's starting to simplify in your mind. (01:41:17): And as you go, usually one informs the other. By the time you finish the accordion for example, you should have a very clear arrow and those clear bookmarks, which is the bow. But really the thing to remember with the bow and arrow, if you can only remember one thing, is switch your mindset from what I want to say to what I want people to remember and limit whatever that is you want them to remember as much as possible and that's going to give you extreme clarity.
turns.zh: 弓箭策略始于一个核心理念：大多数人在准备演讲、会议或汇报时，都陷入了过度关注自身观点的误区。我们需要转变思维模式，少关注自己想说什么，多思考听众需要记住什么。（01:38:51）举个例子：回想你最近参加的全员大会、重要会议、YouTube视频或现场演讲，恐怕很难记住太多内容。事实上，你可能只记住了其中一个要点。这正是我们设计弓箭策略的出发点——因为演讲中只有一个核心观点至关重要，而构建演讲框架时，围绕这个核心展开思考会产生巨大影响。那个核心观点就是你的“箭”。当你确定了这个核心观点后，我建议用一句话来概括——这句话必须是听众离开时唯一能记住的要点。你会满意这样的结果吗？（01:39:37）找到这个核心观点需要花费时间，但一旦确定，它就能激活所有要素。它就像你口袋里的北极星或指南针，随时可用，指引方向。它同样为听众注入清晰的逻辑。（01:39:54）但你不能直接把箭射向听众的面庞。你需要先在弓上搭箭，拉满弓弦。为此，你需要用有趣的轶事、数据支撑，或是感人故事来增强其感染力。核心观点需要权衡利弊，拉满弓弦，让箭射得更远。因此，明确核心观点的过程往往是弓与箭的反复磨合。比如，在第一次写草稿后，你可能先写下初稿的核心观点：“这就是我的核心观点。”然后再进行调整。（01:40:55）最终，你会确定最终的弓和箭的组合。例如，确定了喜欢的轶事、数据点后，你可以用这个故事作为结尾，或是用号召性用语收尾。这样反复打磨，思维会逐渐清晰。（01:41:17）整个过程中，两者相互促进。完成初稿后，核心观点和支撑要素应该清晰明了。但最重要的原则是：如果只能记住一个要点，就要转换思维模式，从“我想说什么”转为“我想让听众记住什么”，尽可能简化核心观点。这将为你的演讲注入极致的清晰度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really helpful. I'm preparing my talk for the summit, and so I'm going to use both of these exercises and what I take away from this last piece is as much as you may want to say a lot of things, really all someone's going to remember, as you said is one thing, if anything, but hopefully they remember that one thing. (01:42:06): So it's essentially what's the one thing you want people to remember and then what are the pieces of support that will convince them that that's right and that's something that'll stick with them?
turns.zh: 这真的很有帮助。我正在为峰会准备演讲，所以我打算用这两个练习方法。通过这次交流，我领悟到的一点是，尽管你可能想说很多东西，但人们真正能记住的只有一件事——即便如此，希望他们至少能记住这一点。（01:42:06）：所以关键在于，你想让人们记住的核心观点是什么？然后用哪些支撑性内容来说服他们，这才是正确的方向。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Exactly. And again, similar to the accordion method, this works in the macro and the micro. So if you have a talk where you're using slides, use it for the whole talk. But then for every single slide, ask yourself what is my one thing? And you might have some support there as well, but if you don't have a one thing for each slide, either the slide shouldn't exist or it should be multiple slides. (01:42:45): The symptom of not having a one thing is usually having a slide that says way too many things. I don't know what data point I want you to remember, so I'm going to put all of it on that slide. I'm not sure which piece of information is more important. So I'm going to write down all of my thoughts and I'm going to go through all of them or hope that you go through all of them and extract what you think is interesting. But the reality is people are just going to zone out if you do that. So if you do that slide by slide, you're going to gain incredible clarity and again, you're going to need less preparation and less memorization.
turns.zh: 没错。和手风琴法类似，这个方法适用于宏观和微观层面。如果你用幻灯片辅助演讲，那就全场都用。但对于每张幻灯片，要问自己：我想让人们记住的核心观点是什么？或许你还能补充一些支撑性内容，但如果每张幻灯片都没有核心观点，要么这张幻灯片不该存在，要么应该拆分成多张幻灯片。（01:42:45）：没有核心观点的症状通常是幻灯片内容过多。我不知道想让你们记住哪条数据点，所以把所有信息都堆到幻灯片上。也不知道哪条信息更重要。所以我就把所有想法都写下来，然后让你们自己去筛选。但现实是，如果你这样做，人们只会走神。所以一张张幻灯片处理下来，既能让你思路清晰，也能减少准备和背诵量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And to build on that, a pro-tip is to make that title of that slide exactly that one thing you want them to take away. Just put it there and tell them exactly what you want them to learn.
turns.zh: 再补充一点，制作幻灯片标题时，要准确传达你希望人们记住的核心观点。直接写上去，告诉他们你想让他们学到什么。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Yes. I love that.
turns.zh: 是的。我很喜欢这个方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. Tristan, we've been on a journey. This was a really unique experimental episode. I had a good time even though I did some hard things, you made me do hard things that are good for me. Is there anything else you want to share before we get to our very exciting lightning round? Is there anything else you want to leave listeners with or a nugget you want to?
turns.zh: 太棒了。特里斯坦，我们完成了一次精彩的探索之旅。这是一期非常独特的实验性节目。尽管我也遇到了一些挑战，但你让我克服了这些挑战，这对我很有益处。还有什么想和听众分享的吗？有什么想留给听众的启发吗？

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: I hope people found value. I mean, we did. This was really a group effort and I really appreciate you working on the agenda, really bringing in the games and trying to make this as practical as possible. I think the only thing I want to leave people with is again, this idea of how transformational tackling speaking can be, and the more constrained you feel with your speaking, the more transformational it will be to your life. So I just want to give this encouragement. It's much, much, much more enjoyable than you think it will be. It can actually be exhilarating and energizing and you feel like you can take over the world once you're on this journey. It's beautiful. And so I just encourage everybody, take the first step and start practicing your speaking.
turns.zh: 希望大家能有所收获。我们的确达成了共识。你为议程做了精心准备，引入了游戏环节，尽可能让内容实用。我想唯一想留给大家的，还是关于演讲变革性的力量。越是觉得演讲受限，它对生活的影响就越深远。所以我想给你们这份鼓励。演讲比你想象的有趣得多、令人振奋得多、充满能量。一旦踏上这条旅程，你会感觉自己能征服全世界。这太美好了。所以我鼓励大家迈出第一步，开始练习演讲。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And I definitely felt that after doing the workshop of just I feel energized, I want to just talk all time, but then I'm like, I need more work. I need more practice. Tristan, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我确实有这种感觉，参加完工作坊后，我感觉精力充沛，恨不得一直讲话，但又觉得自己还需要更多练习。特里斯坦，接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Let's do this lightning round. Here we go.
turns.zh: 开始闪电问答吧。开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Here we go. First question, what are two or three books that you have recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 开始吧。第一个问题：你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: I was given a book by my first coach, Nathan Seward seven years ago called The Big Leap by Gay Hendricks that I've recommended so many times. And it's based on this idea that we tend to self-sabotage ourselves when we experience too much success or too much happiness. And that that's linked to I think five things that would happen to us when we're growing up. One of them is the... What is it, the wild poppy syndrome or something like that. Like the tallest poppy is the one that's cut first. So if you shine in a family of siblings, then anytime you shine too much we're going to say, "Hey, hey, hey, that's not cool for the others." So that's going to be internalized and hardwired in your body and as an adult, as soon as you start shining a little bit too much, you're going to do the same thing to yourself. So the idea is going from having this point above which you can't be happy to turning it into, he calls it an upward-facing spiral with no upper limit. It's a really exciting and empowering book.
turns.zh: 七年前，我的首位教练内森·苏厄德送给我一本书，叫《大跃进》（The Big Leap），作者盖伊·亨德里克斯。这本书我推荐了无数次。书中提出的观点是，当我们取得巨大成功或获得极大快乐时，往往会自我破坏。我认为这与我们成长过程中经历的五件事有关。其中之一是"野生罂粟综合症"之类的说法。比如，最显眼的罂粟花最先被剪掉。所以如果你在兄弟姐妹中表现出色，一旦你过于耀眼，别人就会说："嘿，嘿，嘿，这样做对其他人不公平。"这种观念会深深印在我们的潜意识里，成年后，只要你稍微有点出色，就会对自己下同样的手。书中提倡从无法获得幸福的状态转变为无上限的上升螺旋，这真是一本令人振奋且充满力量的书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: I haven't watched much very recently, but I'll say one of my favorite TV shows of all time is the Peaky Blinders, English show with Cillian Murphy. I'm absolutely obsessed with that movie that show. I think it's a true masterpiece. And I've recently rewatched, so I'll qualify this as recent. I recently rewatched The Nice Guys with Ryan Gosling and Russell Crowe, and I think it's just a brilliant comedy. Brilliant. Another masterpiece, I thought.
turns.zh: 最近我没怎么看电影，但我要说我最喜欢的电视剧之一是《浴血黑帮》（Peaky Blinders），由希里安·墨菲主演的英剧。我对这部剧简直着迷，我认为它是真正的杰作。最近我又重温了一遍。还有《完美保镖》（The Nice Guys），由瑞恩·高斯林和罗素·克劳主演的喜剧片，非常精彩。

turns.en: Do you have a favorite recent product that you have discovered that you really love. Could be an app, it could be something physical.
turns.zh: 你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？可以是应用程序，也可以是实体产品。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: I have a physical product actually right in front of me that was gifted to me by my business partner Michael Gendler, co-founder of Ultraspeaking. This is called an Ember Mug, and this keeps whatever you have in it, warm and it's extraordinary, whether you are a coffee drinker or a tea drinker, you know the feeling of pouring this and sipping it and by the fifth sip, it's cold. This keeps it at whatever temperature you want it to for however long you want. And I absolutely love it. I've been using it basically every day.
turns.zh: 我眼前就有一款实体产品，是我的商业伙伴、Ultraspeaking联合创始人迈克尔·根德勒送给我的。这是一款名为Ember Mug的保温杯，能让饮品保持理想温度，无论是咖啡还是茶。大家都知道倒出饮品后凉得快的问题，它能长时间保持理想温度。我每天都在用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have one of those. I find myself, you could actually control it through the app. You can control the temperature through an app, which I love. I haven't been using mine, but I love the idea. I know a lot of friends love them. Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to, share with friends or family, find useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 我也有一个。通过应用程序就能控制温度，这点我很喜欢。虽然我还没怎么用，但这个概念很棒。我知道很多朋友都喜欢它。最后两个问题。你有没有最喜欢的座右铭，经常回味、与朋友家人分享、在工作或生活中觉得有用的？

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: I think we are too future focused as a species or as a society and as a result, we're always looking for the next thing. So the motto I share with my friends and my business partners and my family the most I think is these are the good old days. And I remind myself, I'll tell you right now for you and for whoever's listening. I mean think about the podcast, it's never going to be this young, it's never going to feel like it feels right now. And it always feels like these things are eternal, but truly one day you're going to look back and you're think, "Man, those were really the good old days." And so I say it right now, enjoy because these are the good old days.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们人类，或者说整个社会，都太过着眼于未来，因此总是在追寻下一个目标。所以我最常跟朋友、合作伙伴和家人分享的座右铭就是："现在就是美好的旧时光。" 我要提醒自己，现在就告诉你们，也告诉所有听众。想想播客吧，它永远不会像现在这样充满活力，也永远不会有现在这样的感觉。人们总觉得这些事物永恒不朽，但终有一天回首往事时，你会感慨："天哪，那真是美好的旧时光啊。" 所以我现在就想说：好好享受吧，因为这些都是美好的旧时光。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. And it's so relevant with a young kid, you're always going to think about, "Oh, they're little." I love that. Final question. You were the fastest person to reach the finals of the world championship of public speaking. I imagine that was quite a journey. I'm curious if there's a story from that experience that comes to mind that's like a wild part of that journey or something that might surprise people.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这句话。这句话对年轻人来说特别贴切，你总会想："他们还小呢。" 我太爱这句话了。最后一个问题。你曾是世界公共演讲锦标赛决赛选手中晋级最快的人。我想这必定是一段不凡的历程。不知你能否分享一段那段旅程中的趣事，或是某个令人惊喜的经历。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Well, the journey lasted almost seven months, and it was the craziest journey of my life. I went into that with no experience whatsoever speaking, so really just a random amateur, and I just climbed the ladder by outworking everybody. The story that came to mind right away was six days before the semifinals. So I'm six days before the semifinals and I've qualified for the semifinals two and a half months ago. So I'm nobody, now I'm going to the semifinals of the world championships of public speaking. So my mind really is struggling to compute, and I had finally unlocked a speech that I thought was worthy of giving on the final stage. You have to show up there for the semifinals with one speech, and then the next day, if ever you win, you're going to the finals and you have to have a brand new speech, a completely different speech that you're going to give on that stage. (01:50:12): So you need two speeches ready to go, and both of those speeches have to be in theory, world-class. I'm six days before. I was struggling at that, really, really struggling to get that speech together. I finally got something and Michael managed to get me. I was flying I think two days later to Vancouver for the semis, and Michael managed to unlock this one opportunity to speak in front of 50 people to give it a try. And so I ran there. I give the speech, and as usual, we film. I film every single speech. I gave more than a hundred speeches over seven months, and I filmed every single speech. And we'd get home, we'd ask everybody for feedback, and I get home and I'm thinking, "Man, something is wrong. Something is wrong." I was so pumped. I wept. I genuinely wept as I wrote the speech because it was so moving. It was all about my life. It was something that I was so connected to. I don't know, probably the emotion of the pressure as well, but that's how much I believed in that speech. (01:51:14): We get home, we put the speech on the computer, and as I get to the most important part of the speech, I see two things happen. So this is the moment where I'm expecting people to pull out their tissues. One person pulls up the agenda for the event that they're at and is starting to look at the agenda. Another person pulls out their phone, another person starts going through their purse, and I'm looking at this, and suddenly I realized, "Oh, this speech, nobody cares about this. This is not a good speech. This is terrible." And then I go through all of these feedbacks. (01:51:53): I have 50 pieces of feedback, and all I'm getting is, "Good luck for the semi-finals. It's going to go great. I thought it was good", and I'm like, "I'm going to humiliate myself. This is terrible." So I had waves of anxiety. I threw my speech away, and in five days from the ground up, I rebuilt a completely new speech that was basically the best of everything I'd explored, everything I'd experimented with over the course of the three months leading up to that, the jokes that worked the best, like a stand-up comic would. I built my special and I focused on different areas like all of the transitions. (01:52:38): And right before the semi-finals, I gave the speech to one person. I was in Vancouver trying to internalize my speech and memorizing it in a plaza where I delimited the size of the stage and I'm just giving my speech out loud to get over the nerves, so I'm ready for the pressure to see if my brain will remember it and everything. (01:53:01): Anyways, I gave it in front of one person who was our district director at Toastmasters, and this is a speech meant for 500 to a thousand people, not one person. So I was scared it would flop. But in the middle of the speech, which is a completely different one, I saw a tear roll down her cheek, and then she just hugged me and said, "You got it. You did it. You did it." I walked out on that stage and I made it, and I won the semi-finals with that speech. (01:53:32): I think to me, that was really the, it showed me that everything I'd done was worth something, that it actually worked. If I was able to build a speech in five days, that could get me a win at the semi-finals of the world championships. That was kind of the ultimate, "Wow, I won." So when I walked into the finals, to me, I felt like I had already won.
turns.zh:
嗯，这次旅程持续了将近七个月，是我人生中最疯狂的一次冒险。当时我毫无演讲经验，完全是个业余新手，全凭勤奋努力才得以晋级。让我立刻浮现脑海的是半决赛前六天的那段经历。距离半决赛还有六天，而我两个半月前才获得晋级资格。当时我还默默无闻，如今却要登上世界演讲锦标赛的半决赛舞台。我的大脑简直难以承受这般反差，终于构思出一篇足以登上决赛舞台的演讲稿。半决赛要求选手仅能携带一篇演讲稿参赛，而次日若获胜则必须更换全新的演讲内容。这意味着我需要准备两篇理论上世界级水平的演讲稿。距离半决赛仅剩六天，我仍在为这篇演讲苦苦挣扎。最终我完成了初稿，迈克尔帮我争取到了在50人面前试讲的机会。试讲结束后，我们拍摄了全过程。在七个月里，我完成了超过100场演讲，每次都进行录像。回家后征求反馈时，却发现大家都无动于衷。看着那份满载人生感悟的演讲稿，我心如刀割。可能是压力过大导致的情绪波动，但那份对演讲的信念始终不减。（01:51:14）回到家后，我将演讲稿上传电脑，当播放到最关键段落时，画面里的人有的翻看活动日程表，有的低头玩手机，有的整理包包。我突然意识到：“天啊，这演讲根本没人感兴趣。这太糟糕了。”随后我仔细研读反馈意见。50条评论里全是“祝你半决赛顺利”、“一定会大放异彩”、“我觉得挺好的”，可我却觉得自己即将出丑。于是我彻底推翻原稿，仅用五天时间重建了一篇新稿，融合了过去三个月探索的精华——成功的笑料、段子手般的节奏感，以及对过渡衔接的精心雕琢。（01:52:38）半决赛前夕，我向一个人试讲。当时我在温哥华的广场上模拟舞台环境，边大声演练边调整节奏，测试记忆力和临场反应。（01:53:01）总之，我在Toastmasters地区总监面前完成了演讲，这场本该面向500至1000人的演讲，
人啊，不是一个人。所以我当时很担心演讲会失败。但在演讲进行到一半时——那是一次完全不同的演讲——我看到她眼角滑落一滴泪水，然后她紧紧拥抱我，说：“你成功了。你做到了。你做到了！” 我走上那个舞台，成功完成了演讲，并凭借那次演讲赢得了半决赛冠军。（01:53:32）对我来说，这真的意义非凡，它让我明白自己所做的一切都是有价值的，都是有效的。如果我能在五天内完成一场演讲，就能在世界锦标赛半决赛中获胜。这简直太不可思议了，“哇，我赢了！” 所以当我走上决赛舞台时，我觉得自己已经是胜利者了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is a story. What an arc. Amazing. I'm so happy you asked that question. Now I just want to watch that speech and I want to learn more about this whole championship of public speaking, which I have no insight into. That could be its own podcast interview. (01:54:13): But Tristan, thank you so much for being here. This was incredible. One of the most interesting episodes I've done. Two final questions. Where can folks learn more about Ultraspeaking? I know you built a page where they could experiment with some of this stuff, so share that. And then how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 哇，这真是个精彩的故事。情节跌宕起伏，太不可思议了。真高兴你提了这个问题。现在我特别想看那段演讲，还想深入了解这项公众演讲锦标赛——我对这方面一无所知。说不定这能单独做成一期播客访谈。（01:54:13）不过特里斯坦，非常感谢你能来参与。这次访谈太棒了，是我做过最有趣的节目之一。最后两个问题：大家在哪里可以了解更多关于Ultraspeaking的信息？我知道你建了一个页面，让人们可以体验一些相关内容，能分享一下链接吗？还有，听众们如何能为你提供帮助呢？

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: If you go to ultraspeaking. com/Lenny, so ultra like U-L-T-R-A ultraspeaking.com/Lenny, we put together, you have five emails that go deep into a bunch of the things that we've talked here. You can also just go to Ultraspeaking.com where you'll get access to a bunch of the games for free, and you can check out everything else that we do. If you want to follow me or hit me up or ask me questions about this podcast, you can do that on Twitter @Montebello, M-O-N-T-E-B-E-L-L-O. And how can listeners be useful to me? Well, first of all, if you made it to here, then I really appreciate you. Thank you. Thank you for being here with us, and what I would love for you to do is to apply this. We said in the beginning, you can't get better at speaking without speaking, and another piece of that puzzle is you want to do the thing that you're trying to get better at. So if you're nervous speaking in front of people, you want to speak in front of people as part of your practice. So the way you could be useful to me is introduce these games to somebody else. Try them for yourself, practice them with somebody else. Go through the accordion method with a friend. Try conductor, and when you succeed and when you have an awesome experience, then you can tell the world that Ultraspeaking helped you do that, and that would be huge.
turns.zh: 访问ultraspeaking.com/Lenny（注意正确拼写），你会看到五封邮件，深入解析我们在节目中讨论的诸多内容。你也可以直接访问Ultraspeaking.com，免费获取一系列游戏资源，并了解我们的其他服务。如果想关注我、与我互动或向我提问，请在Twitter上@Montebello（M-O-N-T-E-B-E-L-L-O）联系我。听众如何能为我提供帮助呢？首先，如果你能耐心听完这段内容，我真心感激。感谢你的支持。希望你能将所学付诸实践。正如我们开场提到的，不练习就无法提高口语能力，而关键在于你要持续练习。比如，如果你对在众人面前发言感到紧张，那就多参与公众演讲活动。通过介绍这些游戏资源，亲自体验并与他人练习，你就能为我贡献力量。比如，与朋友一起尝试手风琴练习法，或体验指挥者模式。当你成功时，不妨告诉全世界Ultraspeaking帮助了你，那将意义非凡。

turns.en: Awesome. Tristan, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。特里斯坦，非常感谢你的到来。

turns.speaker: Tristan de Montebello
turns.en: Thanks, Lenny. It was an honor.

You can find all past episodes or learn more about the show at LennysPodcast.com. See you in the next episode.
